questions.questionText: What direction does the first principal component (PC1) point in?
options: The direction with the least variance in the data
The direction of maximum variance in the data
Always the same direction as the first original feature
A random direction chosen for initialization
questions.correctAnswer: The direction of maximum variance in the data
questions.explanation: PC1 is defined as the axis along which the data is most spread out; each subsequent component captures the next-most variance while staying orthogonal to the previous ones.

questions.questionText: Why should features typically be standardized (scaled) before applying PCA?
options: PCA doesn't work on unscaled data at all
A feature with a much larger numeric range would dominate the variance calculation regardless of its actual importance
Standardization is only needed for classification, not PCA
It has no effect on PCA's results
questions.correctAnswer: A feature with a much larger numeric range would dominate the variance calculation regardless of its actual importance
questions.explanation: Since PCA operates on variance, an unscaled feature measured in large numbers would swamp the calculation, just like the feature-scaling issue with KNN's distance calculation.

questions.questionText: What does a principal component's "explained variance ratio" tell you?
options: How accurate a downstream model will be
What fraction of the total variance in the dataset that single component accounts for
How many original features were dropped
The correlation between two specific original features
questions.correctAnswer: What fraction of the total variance in the dataset that single component accounts for
questions.explanation: Summing explained variance ratios across the components you keep tells you how much of the original information survived the dimensionality reduction.
